name: OpenJDK HotSpot (Java 27): LangArena Binarytrees::Obj
baseline: C++ (std::make_unique tree nodes, g++ 16 and clang++ 22) and C (malloc'd nodes); best C/C++ configuration is C++/G++/Fast at 2.098 s
workload: Allocate, sum and free a complete binary tree of individually allocated nodes, repeated per iteration (idiomatic object version of binary-trees).
claimed_speedup: Java/OpenJDK 0.479 s vs C++/G++ 2.101 s (prod, -O2), C++/G++ -O3 'Fast' 2.098 s (best of all 16 C/C++ configurations), C/Clang 2.482 s: about 4.4x faster than C++/G++ and 5.2x faster than C/Clang (derived from page data). Kotlin/JVM 0.479 s, Scala/JVM 0.48 s, GraalVM JIT 0.807 s.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++: Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk). Headline 'prod' build is -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer (not -O3). The same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops, thin LTO), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, full LTO) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus profile) variants of every C and C++ benchmark; all 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ configurations were compared here. Managed side: Temurin OpenJDK 27+35 with -Xmx2g, dotnet 11.0.100-rc.1 (Release), Julia 1.13.1 with --threads=16 (versions from the results file).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Inferred from the sources, not stated by the suite: the C++ tree allocates every node with make_unique (one malloc/free per node and recursive destruction), while HotSpot allocates short-lived objects by pointer bump in thread-local buffers and reclaims them with a generational GC. The suite's own index-based Arena variant reverses the result (C/Gcc/Fast 0.255 s vs Java 1.086 s).
tradeoffs: Peak RSS about 892 MB for Java vs about 66 MB for C/Clang on this test; needs a JVM and warm-up; other runtimes do not share the win on this test (C#/JIT 4.373 s, Julia 2.185 s).
caveats: The win is allocation-strategy specific: a C/C++ arena or pool allocator beats the JVM here, so 'Java beats C++' only holds against per-node malloc/free. LangArena's own README calls it 'a subjective benchmark', and the author says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. The suite publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance), and JIT languages get a separate warm-up phase, so startup is excluded. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3, LTO, PGO and fast-math variants were also compared and still lose on this test. Rows were selected by this agent as the tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most other tests in the suite go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and the Binarytrees::Arena variant). The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.

name: dotnet JIT (C# staged Brainfuck) in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C++ (g++ 16.1.0 and clang++ 22.1.8) and C (gcc, clang) Brainfuck interpreters in the same suite
workload: Run two Brainfuck programs (bench.b and mandel.b) end to end, including start-up and JIT time; the staged variant turns each program into a chain of generic struct types that RyuJIT compiles at run time.
claimed_speedup: bench.b: C# (Staged)/.NET Core 0.373 s vs C++/g++ 1.097 s, C/gcc 1.112 s, C++/clang++ 1.167 s. mandel.b: C# (Staged) 2.917 s vs C++/g++ 10.143 s, C/gcc 12.544 s, C++/clang++ 12.803 s. About 2.9x and 3.5x faster than the best C/C++ row (derived from page data). Scala (Staged) 0.409 s and 7.118 s also beat C++.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ built with COMMON_FLAGS -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk), -std=c23 and -std=c++23 (clang++ with libc++); gcc/g++ 16.1.0, clang 22.1.8; .NET Core 10.0.100 (versions table in the README).
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G, Docker image Debian forky/sid (README Environment section)
why_faster: Runtime specialization: bf-staged.cs builds one closed generic type per Brainfuck instruction sequence (MakeGenericType over static abstract interface methods) so the .NET JIT compiles and inlines the whole program at run time, while the C and C++ versions interpret the program text.
tradeoffs: Needs the .NET runtime and JIT at run time; memory 36.6 MiB for C# (Staged) vs 3.4 MiB for C++/g++ on bench.b. The plain (non-staged) C# row is slower than C++ (bench.b 1.280 s vs 1.097 s).
caveats: Not the same algorithm: staged compilation of the program versus an interpreter loop, so it shows what run-time specialization buys, not that C# generates faster code than C++ for the same source. A C++ implementation that also compiles the program (templates, closure compilation, a JIT) would be expected to close the gap. The suite says its implementations are 'written as the average software developer would write them', and the staged variants are separately contributed. Medians with median absolute deviation are published, but the README says the published measurements are taken semi-manually via shell because a full Docker update takes days.
